wrong_text: The ice sheet reached as far south as the Bristol Channel and the Thames Valley — a line running roughly from the Severn Estuary to north London.
problem: This conflates two different glaciations. The Devensian (last glacial maximum, ~27,000–20,000 years ago) reached the Bristol Channel in the west but only approximately the Humberside/The Wash line in the east — NOT the Thames Valley or north London. The Thames Valley ice is from the far older Anglian glaciation (~450,000 years ago). Teaching the Thames Valley as the LGM limit is a significant factual error. Source: antarcticglaciers.org LGM British-Irish Ice Sheet; internetgeography.net; Quaternary Research Group Cambridge.
correction: The ice sheet reached as far south as the Bristol Channel in the west and roughly the Humberside coast in the east. Everything north of a line from the Severn Estuary to the Vale of York — Scotland, most of Wales, northern England and all of Ireland — lay beneath ice up to 1 km thick in places.

wrong_text: the ice carried them uphill from the south and deposited them 3–4 metres higher than the bedrock below
problem: The Norber erratics are perched on limestone pedestals 30–50 cm (not 3–4 metres) high. The 'higher' in the classic description refers to the pedestal height caused by differential weathering, which is approximately 30–50 cm according to Wikipedia and dalesrocks.org.uk. The 3–4 metre figure does not appear in any authoritative source and is wrong by an order of magnitude.
correction: the ice carried them uphill from the south and deposited them on the limestone pavement. The limestone pavement has been dissolved away around the protected bases of the boulders, leaving them perched on limestone pedestals up to 50 cm high.

wrong_text: a 1,880-tonne erratic of Ennerdale Granophyre sitting on Borrowdale Volcanic rock
problem: Two errors: (1) Rock type — the Bowder Stone is andesite lava from the Borrowdale Volcanic Group, not Ennerdale Granophyre. These are different rock bodies; the Ennerdale Granophyre is a separate intrusion near Ennerdale. Wikipedia and the Heritage Journal confirm the stone is andesite. (2) Erratic status — modern geology (confirmed by multiple geological sources) considers the Bowder Stone a rockfall from Bowder Crag directly above, not a glacial erratic. Describing it as an erratic in a lesson on glacial deposition is geologically incorrect and potentially misleading at GCSE level. Weight is also approximately 2,000 tonnes/tons in most sources, not 1,880 tonnes. Source: Wikipedia Bowder Stone; Heritage Journal 2023.
correction: the Bowder Stone in Borrowdale, a large boulder of andesite lava from the Borrowdale Volcanic Group, traditionally cited as an erratic but now considered by geologists to be a rockfall from the Bowder Crag directly above, dislodged after the glacier retreated

wrong_text: Fix the Fells project has restored over 200 km of upland paths since 2003
problem: Fix the Fells was established on 18 August 2001 (not 2003). By its own published figures it has repaired over 200 paths covering more than 400 km (not 200 km). The lesson states '200 km' in the key fact box, conclusion, knowledge check, flashcard and exam tip — all need updating. The '2003' date is wrong throughout. Source: fixthefells.co.uk; Wikipedia Fix the Fells; Lake District National Park '15 years of volunteers' press release (counting from 2001).
correction: Fix the Fells project has restored over 400 km of upland paths since 2001

wrong_text: The Lake District receives around 20 million visitors per year
problem: Official Cumbria Tourism figures: 17.73 million visitors in 2024; 18.11 million in 2023. The 20 million figure is outdated. The correct current figure is approximately 18 million. Source: cumbriatourism.org 2024 annual report; lakedistrict.gov.uk/learning/factstourism.
correction: The Lake District receives around 18 million visitors per year
